title: The Discount Stack: Why a Record Black Friday Rarely Means a More Profitable Christmas for E-Commerce Retailers
linkedin:
Black Friday planning is already locked in for most Australian e-commerce retailers. Stock is ordered, the marketing calendar is set, and the November revenue number looks strong on paper.

What rarely gets the same scrutiny is the margin sitting underneath that number.

We see three costs quietly compound in exactly the weeks revenue looks healthiest.

The discount stack: a headline percentage off sits on top of a free shipping threshold, an affiliate commission, and payment fees that rise with volume. Stacked together, the real discount given away is often much deeper than the number in the marketing brief.

Customer acquisition cost that does not take a Christmas break: every retailer competing for the same Australian shoppers in the same six weeks pushes cost per click up, so the customer acquired in peak season often costs more to win than the one acquired in a quiet month.

The return rate you do not see until January: gift and impulse purchases made during a sale carry a structurally higher return rate. Revenue books in November. The refund lands in January, once the return window closes.

None of this argues against running the sale. It argues for stress-testing contribution margin, acquisition cost and return rate before the campaign is locked in, not after the results land.

Quick one for anyone running an online store gearing up for Black Friday and Christmas: have you actually worked out what a 20 percent off sale costs once you add free shipping, an affiliate commission and payment fees on top?

We keep seeing the same pattern. Revenue climbs in November. The margin quietly does not, because the real discount stack is deeper than the headline number, ad costs spike as everyone bids for the same shoppers, and a chunk of the sale revenue comes back as returns in January.

Worth doing that maths before the sale goes live, not after it ends.

For any Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales or Victoria business selling online, Black Friday and Christmas trading plans are likely already locked in for this year. Stock is ordered, ad budgets are set, and the revenue target for November and December is probably looking strong.

What is worth checking now, while there is still time to adjust, is the profit sitting underneath that revenue number. A Black Friday discount rarely stands alone. The headline percentage off usually sits on top of a free shipping threshold, an affiliate commission and payment processing fees that rise as sales volume climbs, and stacked together the real discount given away is often deeper than anyone intended.

Advertising costs add another layer. Every online retailer is competing for the same shoppers in the same narrow window, which pushes up the cost of winning a customer right when volume is highest. And a share of peak season revenue typically comes back as returns in January, once gift and impulse purchases make their way home.

None of this means skipping the sale. It means testing the real margin sitting underneath the revenue target before the campaign locks in, not after the results land.
